abstract: Slender, flexible bodies allow animals such as millipedes to regularly traverse heterogeneous, uneven terrain and complex obstacles by using their body's compliance to conform to the terrain. Orchestrating a slender body's many degrees of freedom poses a control challenge, with possible strategies ranging in complexity and cost, from complex muscle actuation patterns to simple passive compliance. Here we investigate these behavioral strategies by examining American giant millipedes (Narceus americanus) bridging between terrains of different heights. We model millipede trunk mechanics using Cosserat rods and compare resulting equilibrium configurations with experimental data to determine bending stiffnesses that best recreates their posture and test for regional and temporal variations. We find that a highly compliant, passive rod best captures millipede poses during periods where its middle section is unsupported. This supports the hypothesis that millipedes do not strongly actively stiffen their trunk during terrain bridging, relying instead on their body's passive compliance.
